The acceleration, a ms-2 , of a particle moving in a horizontal line at time t seconds, t ≥ 0 , is
given by a = - (1+v) where v ms-1 is the particle’s velocity and v > -1.
At t = 0 , the particle is at a fixed origin O and has initial velocity v0 ms-1 .
(a)
By solving an appropriate differential equation, show that the particle’s velocity at time t
is given by v ( t ) = (1 + v0) e-t - 1 .
[6]
(b)
Initially at O, the particle moves in the positive direction until it reaches its maximum
displacement from O. The particle then returns to O.
Let s metres represent the particle’s displacement from O and smax its maximum
displacement from O.
(i)
Show that the time T taken for the particle to reach smax satisfies the
equation eT = 1 + v0 .
(ii)
By solving an appropriate differential equation and using the result from part
(b) (i), find an expression for smax in terms of v0 .
[7]
Let v (T - k) represent the particle’s velocity k seconds before it reaches smax , where
v (T - k) = (1 + v0) e-(T - k) - 1 .
(c)
By using the result to part (b) (i), show that v (T - k) = ek - 1 .
[2]
Similarly, let v (T + k) represent the particle’s velocity k seconds after it reaches smax .
(d)
Deduce a similar expression for v (T + k) in terms of k .
[2]
(e)
Hence, show that v (T - k) + v (T + k) ≥ 0 .

This question asks you to find the probability of graphs of randomly generated
quadratic functions having a specified number of x-intercepts.
In parts (a) – (f), consider quadratic functions, f (x) = ax2 + bx + c , whose coefficients, a , b
and c , are randomly generated in turn by rolling an unbiased six-sided die three times and
reading off the value shown on the uppermost face of the die.
For example, rolling a 2 , 3 and 5 in turn generates the quadratic function f (x) = 2x2 + 3x + 5 .
(a)
Explain why there are 216 possible quadratic functions that can be generated using
this method.

The set of coefficients, a = 1 , b = 4 and c = 4 , is randomly generated to form the

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 5] Consider the function f(x) = 3(x − 2)(x − q), where x ∈ ℝ and q is a real constant. The axis of symmetry of the graph of f has equation x = 4. (a) Show that q = 6. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of f. [2] (c) Hence, write down the range of f. [1]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: Let f(x)=3(x-2)(x-q). Its zeros are 2 and q, so the axis of symmetry is x=(2+q)/2. Since this is x=4, q=6. Thus f(4)=3(4-2)(4-6)=-12, giving vertex (4,-12). The parabola opens upwards, so the range is f(x)≥-12, i.e. [-12,∞).
records.consensusRationale: The axis of symmetry, vertex, and range are determined from a quadratic; no graph-transformation or inverse-function operation is independently marked.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 15] Consider the function f(x) = ax³ + bx² + cx + d, where x ∈ ℝ and where a, b, c and d are real constants. The graph of f has a point of inflexion at (−2, −2c + d + 24). (a) Show that a = 3/2 and b = 9. [6] It is given that the tangents to the graph of f at x = −3 and x = k are horizontal. (b) (i) Show that c = 27/2. (ii) Find the value of k. (iii) State whether f has a local maximum or a local minimum at x = k, justifying your answer. [7] The graph of f intersects the y-axis at the point P. (c) Show that the tangent to the graph of f at x = −3 passes through P. [2]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: Write f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d. Since the inflection point has x-coordinate −2, f''(−2)=0: −12a+2b=0, so b=6a. Its y-coordinate condition gives f(−2)=−2c+d+24. But f(−2)=−8a+4b−2c+d=16a−2c+d, hence 16a=24 and a=3/2, b=9. (b)(i) The horizontal tangent at x=−3 gives f'(−3)=0. Since f'(x)=3ax^2+2bx+c, 27a−6b+c=0, so c=27/2. (ii) f'(x)=(9/2)x^2+18x+27/2=(9/2)(x+3)(x+1), so the other horizontal tangent is at k=−1. (iii) f''(x)=9x+18, so f''(−1)=9>0; therefore f has a local minimum at x=−1. (c) The y-intercept is P=(0,d). At x=−3, f(−3)=d, and f'(−3)=0, so the tangent there is horizontal, hence its equation is y=d and it passes through P.
records.consensusRationale: The inflection condition, horizontal tangents, local-minimum test, and tangent-line conclusion are all differentiation and its applications.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 19] (a) Prove the identity cot 2θ = 1/2(cot θ − 1/cot θ). [3] (b) Hence, solve the equation cot 2θ = (3/2) cot θ(cot² θ − 1) for 0 < θ < π where θ ≠ π/2. [6] (c) By differentiating both sides of the identity in part (a), show that 4 cosec² 2θ = cosec² θ + sec² θ. [5] Consider the right-angled triangle ΔPQR, where R̂PQ = π/2. PR = cosec θ, QR = 2 cosec 2θ, where 0 < θ < π/2 and all lengths are given in metres. This is shown in the following diagram (diagram not to scale): P is the lower-left vertex, Q is directly above P, R is to the right of P; angle QPR is the right angle, side PR is labelled cosec θ, and hypotenuse QR is labelled 2cosec 2θ. QR has length L metres and ΔPQR has area A square metres. (d) Calculate the ratio L : A in the form n : 1, where n ∈ ℤ. [5]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: (a) tan(2θ)=2tanθ/(1−tan²θ), so cot(2θ)=(1−tan²θ)/(2tanθ)=1/2(cotθ−tanθ)=1/2(cotθ−1/cotθ). (b) Let t=cotθ. Then (t^2−1)/(2t)=(3/2)t(t^2−1). Since t≠0 in the stated domain, (t^2−1)(3t^2−1)=0. Thus cotθ=±1 or ±1/√3. For 0<θ<π and θ≠π/2, θ=π/4, π/3, 2π/3, 3π/4. (c) Differentiate the identity in (a): −2cosec²(2θ)=1/2(−cosec²θ−sec²θ). Multiplying by −2 gives 4cosec²(2θ)=cosec²θ+sec²θ. (d) In the right triangle, QR=2cosec(2θ) and PR=cosecθ. By Pythagoras and part (c), PQ²=4cosec²(2θ)−cosec²θ=sec²θ, so PQ=secθ. Thus L=2cosec(2θ)=1/(sinθ cosθ), while A=(1/2)(secθ)(cosecθ)=1/(2sinθ cosθ). Therefore L:A=2:1, so n=2.
records.consensusRationale: Parts (a), (b), and the final ratio use trig identities/equations and a right triangle; part (c) independently differentiates the identity for five marks.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 18] Rowan is investigating the spread of an infection through a population of rabbits. He models N, the number (in thousands) of infected rabbits in the population, at time t days. Rowan models the spread of the infection by the differential equation dN/dt = k(−3 + 4N − N²), where t ≥ 0 and k ∈ ℝ⁺. Initially, 1500 rabbits are infected. (a) Express 1/(−3 + 4x − x²) in the form A/(x − 1) + B/(3 − x), where A, B ∈ ℝ. [3] (b) Hence, show that ln((N − 1)/(3 − N)) = 2kt − ln p, where p ∈ ℝ⁺ is a constant to be determined. [8] (c) Find an expression for N in the form N = (a + b e⁻²ᵏᵗ)/(1 + c e⁻²ᵏᵗ), where a, b, c ∈ ℤ. [5] According to Rowan's model, the number of infected rabbits approaches a limit, L, over the long term. (d) Find the value of L. [2]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: Separate variables: dN/[−3+4N−N^2]=k dt. Since −3+4N−N^2=(N−1)(3−N), partial fractions give 1/[(N−1)(3−N)]=1/2(N−1)+1/2(3−N). Integrating, (1/2)ln((N−1)/(3−N))=kt+C. Initially N=1.5, so the ratio is 1/3; hence ln((N−1)/(3−N))=2kt−ln3, or (N−1)/(3−N)=e^{2kt}/3. Solving gives N=3(1+e^{2kt})/(3+e^{2kt})=(3+3e^{−2kt})/(1+3e^{−2kt}), which has the requested integer-coefficient form. As t→∞ (k>0), e^{−2kt}→0, so N→3. Since N is measured in thousands, the limiting number is L=3000 rabbits.
records.consensusRationale: The entire question separates and solves a logistic differential equation, derives its closed form, and finds its long-term equilibrium.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 5] A particle P is travelling along a straight line, with displacement measured relative to a point O on the line. The velocity, v m s⁻¹, of the particle at time t seconds is given by v = 1/(t + 1) + e⁻ᵗ, where t ≥ 0. (a) Find ∫(1/(t + 1) + e⁻ᵗ) dt. [2] Initially the particle is at O. (b) Find an expression for the displacement, s metres, in terms of t. [3]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: Since v=ds/dt=1/(t+1)+e^{-t}, integrate: s=ln(t+1)-e^{-t}+C. Initially s(0)=0, hence 0=0-1+C and C=1. Therefore s=ln(t+1)-e^{-t}+1 metres (t≥0).
records.consensusRationale: The two independent blind passes agree exactly after runtime normalization.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 7] (a) Show that log₂₅(81x) = log₅ 9 + log₂₅ x for x > 0. [4] (b) Hence, solve the equation log₅ ∛x = log₂₅(81x²) − log₅ 4, where x > 0. [3]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: (a) Using change of base, log_25(81x)=(1/2)log_5(81x)=(1/2)[2log_5 9+log_5 x]=log_5 9+(1/2)log_5 x. (b) Also log_5(cube root of x)=(1/3)log_5 x. Hence (1/3)log_5 x=log_5 x+log_5(9/4). Therefore -(2/3)log_5 x=log_5(9/4), so log_5 x=log_5((4/9)^(3/2)) and x=(4/9)^(3/2)=8/27.
records.consensusRationale: Both the change-of-base identity and the subsequent solve are explicitly logarithm-rule work.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 9] Consider two events, A and B. It is given that P(A ∩ B′) = (5 + x)/24, P(A ∩ B) = (7 − x)/12 and P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1/6, where 0 ≤ x ≤ 7. (a) Show that P(A) = (19 − x)/24. [3] It is given that A and B are independent. (b) Find the possible values of x. [6]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: The given regions are P(A∩B')=(5+x)/24, P(A∩B)=(7-x)/12 and P(A'∩B')=1/6. (a) P(A)=P(A∩B')+P(A∩B)=(5+x)/24+2(7-x)/24=(19-x)/24. (b) The remaining region is P(A'∩B)=1-[ (5+x)/24+(7-x)/12+1/6]=(1+x)/24. Hence P(B)=P(A∩B)+P(A'∩B)=(7-x)/12+(1+x)/24=(15-x)/24. Independence gives (7-x)/12=((19-x)/24)((15-x)/24). Therefore 48(7-x)=(19-x)(15-x), so x^2+14x-51=0=(x-3)(x+17). Since 0≤x≤7, the only possible value is x=3.
records.consensusRationale: The four event regions, independence equation, and admissible solution are a probability-model calculation without a conditional-probability step.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 8] Consider the polynomial p(z) = 3z⁵ − 7z⁴ + cz³ + dz² + ez − 26, where z ∈ ℂ and c, d, e ∈ ℝ. Three of the roots of p(z) are 1/3, a − i, 2 + bi, where a, b ∈ ℝ, b > 1. (a) By considering the sum and the product of the roots of p(z), (i) show that a = −1; (ii) find the value of b. [5] (b) Show that p(z) = (Az + B)(z² + Cz + D)(z² + Ez + F), where A, B, C, D, E, F are integers to be determined. [3]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: Because p has real coefficients, the conjugates a+i and 2-bi are also roots. The five roots are therefore 1/3, a−i, a+i, 2+bi, 2−bi. (a)(i) The sum of roots is 7/3. Thus 1/3+2a+4=7/3, giving a=−1. (ii) The product of roots is −(constant)/(leading coefficient)=26/3. Hence (1/3)(a^2+1)(b^2+4)=26/3. With a=−1, 2(b^2+4)=26, so b^2=9; since b>1, b=3. (b) Pairing conjugate roots, p(z)=3(z−1/3)[(z+1)^2+1][(z−2)^2+9]=(3z−1)(z^2+2z+2)(z^2−4z+13).
records.consensusRationale: Real-coefficient conjugate roots, sums/products of complex roots, and factorization into a linear and two quadratic factors are the marked work.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 7] A group of 52 students have their heights measured in cm. The cumulative frequency graph for the heights of the students is shown in the question paper. The graph has height/cm on the horizontal axis from 150 to 180 and cumulative frequency on the vertical axis from 0 to 55. (a) Use the graph to find an estimate of the median height. [2] (This question continues on the following page.) The heights of the students are shown in the following frequency table, where p, q ∈ ℕ. Table columns: Height (h cm), Frequency. Rows: 155 ≤ h < 160, 3; 160 ≤ h < 165, 8; 165 ≤ h < 170, 14; 170 ≤ h < 175, p; 175 ≤ h < 180, q. (b) (i) Find the value of p and the value of q. (ii) Use the frequency table to find an estimate of the mean height, giving your answer to 4 significant figures. [5]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: (a) There are 52 students, so the median is at cumulative frequency 52/2 = 26. Reading the cumulative-frequency graph at CF = 26 gives an estimated median height of 170.5 cm. (b)(i) The first three frequencies total 3 + 8 + 14 = 25. Hence p = 42 - 25 = 17 and q = 52 - 42 = 10. (b)(ii) Use class midpoints 157.5, 162.5, 167.5, 172.5, 177.5. The grouped estimate is [(157.5)(3) + (162.5)(8) + (167.5)(14) + (172.5)(17) + (177.5)(10)]/52 = 169.673... cm, so the estimated mean is 169.7 cm (4 s.f.).
records.consensusRationale: The two independent blind passes agree exactly after runtime normalization.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 13] At the start of 2026, Lavinia receives a gift of $15 000. She wants to buy a boat which costs $28 000 at the start of 2026. On 1 January 2026, Lavinia invests her money in a bank account which pays interest at a nominal annual rate of 4.8%, compounded quarterly. The interest is paid into her account at the end of each quarter. She makes no further deposits to, or withdrawals from, the account. (a) Find the amount of money Lavinia will have in her bank account on 1 January 2031. Give your answer correct to the nearest dollar. [3] (b) Show that Lavinia will first have more than $28 000 in her bank account during the year 2039. [3] The cost of the boat at the start of 2026 was $28 000, and it depreciates at a constant annual rate of r%. After one year, the value of the boat is $26 222. (c) Find the value of r. [2] Due to this depreciation, Lavinia will be able to buy the boat before 2039. She will buy the boat as soon as she has enough money in her bank account. (d) Determine the year during which Lavinia will buy the boat. [5]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: Quarterly interest of 4.8% gives a quarterly multiplier 1.012. (a) Five years is 20 quarters: 15000(1.012)^20 = 19041.515..., so $19,042 to the nearest dollar. (b) After n years the balance is 15000(1.012)^(4n). Requiring it to exceed 28000 gives n > ln(28000/15000)/[4 ln(1.012)] = 13.0811... years after 1 January 2026, so the first time is during the year 2039. (c) One year of depreciation gives 28000(1-r/100)=26222, so r/100=1-26222/28000=0.0635 and r=6.35. (d) After n years compare 15000(1.012)^(4n) with 28000(0.9365)^n. Equality occurs at n=ln(28000/15000)/ln[(1.012)^4/0.9365]=5.50785... years after 1 January 2026. The crossover is approximately mid-2031, so she buys during 2031.
records.consensusRationale: Quarterly compound interest and annual depreciation are geometric-growth models; logarithms determine the first crossing and purchase year.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 21] The function f is defined as f(x) = (x² + ax + b)/(x + 1), where x ≠ −1 and a, b ∈ ℤ. First consider the case where f(x) is finite. (a) (i) Show that b = a − 1. (ii) Find lim as x tends to −1 of f(x) in terms of a. [4] Now consider the case where the graph of f has a vertical asymptote, an oblique asymptote with equation y = x − 4, and at least one point of zero gradient. (b) Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote. [1] (c) Show that a = −3. [3] (d) Show that b ≥ −3. [6] (e) In the case where a = −3 and b = 1, (i) sketch the graph of y = f(|x|), showing the asymptotes with their equations, the y-axis intercept, and the coordinates of any local maximum or minimum points. (ii) Solve f(|x|) < f(x). [7]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: f(x)=(x²+ax+b)/(x+1), x≠-1. (a)(i) For a finite limit at x→-1, the numerator must vanish at -1: 1-a+b=0, so b=a-1. (a)(ii) With b=a-1, x²+ax+a-1=(x+1)(x+a-1), hence f(x)=x+a-1 for x≠-1 and the limit is a-2. (b) An oblique asymptote is y=x-4, so a-1=-4 and a=-3. (c) Polynomial division gives f(x)=x-4+(b+4)/(x+1). Since the vertical asymptote is x=-1, b+4≠0. A zero-gradient point requires f'(x)=1-(b+4)/(x+1)²=0, so b+4=(x+1)²>0; hence b>-4. (d) The integer values satisfying b>-4 are b≥-3, so the result required is b≥-3 (with least possible value b=-3). (e)(i) With a=-3,b=1, f(x)=x-4+5/(x+1). Therefore f(|x|)=(|x|²-3|x|+1)/(|x|+1). Its asymptotes are y=x-4 as x→+∞ and y=-x-4 as x→-∞. The x-intercepts are x=±(3-√5)/2 and x=±(3+√5)/2; the y-intercept is (0,1). For x≥0, f'(x)=1-5/(x+1)², giving minima at x=√5-1 and x=1-√5, both with y=2√5-5; by the cusp/even symmetry, (0,1) is a local maximum. (e)(ii) Comparing the two expressions and respecting x≠-1 gives f(|x|)<f(x) precisely for -1<x<0.
records.consensusRationale: The absolute-value graph, asymptotes, intercepts, and extrema make graph transformations primary; stationary points use differentiation and the final seven-mark comparison is an explicit inequality.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 4] Consider a function f which has a first derivative given by f′(x) = x² − x − 1, where x ∈ ℝ. Find the range of values of x for which f is decreasing. [4]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: f'(x) = x^2 - x - 1. The function is decreasing where f'(x) < 0. The roots of x^2 - x - 1 = 0 are x = (1 ± √5)/2, and the quadratic has positive leading coefficient, so it is negative between the roots. Therefore f is decreasing for (1 - √5)/2 < x < (1 + √5)/2.
records.consensusRationale: The two independent blind passes agree exactly after runtime normalization.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 6] A Ferris wheel with radius 20 metres rotates at a constant speed. The centre of the wheel is 23 metres above the ground, as shown in the following diagram. P is a point on the wheel. The wheel starts moving with P at the lowest point and completes one revolution in 4 minutes. The diagram is not to scale. The diagram shows a circular Ferris wheel, with its centre 23 m above the ground and radius 20 m; the point P is initially at the lowest point, 3 m above the ground. The height, h metres, of P above the ground after t minutes is given by h = a − b cos(ct)°, where a, b, c ∈ ℤ⁺; the degree symbol is printed in the source. (a) Find the value of a, the value of b and the value of c. [4] The height can also be given as h(t) = a − b sin(c(t + d))°, where d ∈ ℤ⁺. (b) Find the smallest positive value of d. [2]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: The wheel has radius 20 m and its centre is 23 m above the ground, so the midline is a = 23 and the amplitude is b = 20. It starts at the lowest point, where h(0) = 3. The source prints a degree symbol after each trigonometric argument, so one revolution in 4 minutes gives 360/c = 4 and hence c = 90. Thus a = 23, b = 20 and c = 90. For the alternative form, sin(90(t + 1)°) = sin(90t° + 90°) = cos(90t°), so the smallest positive value is d = 1.
records.consensusRationale: The sinusoidal height model is determined from midline, amplitude, period, and phase translation, all graph-transformation features.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 7] Consider the function g defined as g(x) = x³ − 3x + 2 sin x, where x ∈ ℝ. The graph of g has a local maximum at point A and a local minimum at point B. The line (AB) passes through the origin at O, (0, 0). The region R is enclosed by the graph of g and the line segment [OB], as shown on the following diagram. The diagram shows the curve y = g(x), with A on the negative-x side, B on the positive-x side, O at the origin, and the straight line segment from O to B; R is the region between the curve and [OB]. (a) Find the coordinates of point A and the coordinates of point B. [2] (b) Find the area of R. [5]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: g(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2 sin x, so g'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 + 2 cos x. Solving g'(x)=0 gives x = ±0.700108395... . Since g is odd, A = (-0.700108..., 0.468564643...) and B = (0.700108..., -0.468564643...). Let x_B = 0.700108395... . The line segment OB is y = mx, where m = g(x_B)/x_B = -0.669274424... . The region R is between the curve and OB for 0 ≤ x ≤ x_B, so its area is |∫_0^(x_B) [g(x)-mx] dx| = 0.040687145... . Therefore the area of R is approximately 0.0407 square units.
records.consensusRationale: Coordinates of extrema require solving g′=0, while the enclosed region is found from a definite integral against the chord; both are independently marked.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 7] A large group of adults have their heights measured. The heights of the adults are normally distributed with mean μ and standard deviation σ cm. The probability that one of the adults chosen at random has a height greater than 171 cm is 0.4. If one of the adults with a height greater than 171 cm is chosen at random, the probability that their height is greater than 175 cm is 0.35. Find the value of μ and the value of σ. [7]
records.consensusRationale: The parameters come from two normal tail probabilities, with the second obtained from the explicitly conditional height statement.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 4] The air inside an airtight syringe is compressed so that its volume, V cm³, decreases. The air pressure, P newtons per cm², within the syringe is inversely proportional to the volume so that PV = 135. At a given time, the volume of the air is 20 cm³ and is decreasing at a rate of 8 cm³ per minute. Find the rate of increase of the air pressure at this time. [4] The diagram shows an airtight syringe containing air, with the plunger being pushed in.
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: PV = 135, so differentiating with respect to t gives V(dP/dt) + P(dV/dt)=0. At the instant V=20 cm³, dV/dt = -8 cm³ min⁻¹, and P=135/20=27/4. Therefore 20(dP/dt) + (27/4)(-8)=0, so 20(dP/dt)=54 and dP/dt = 2.7 N cm⁻² min⁻¹.
records.consensusRationale: Related rates are solved by differentiating PV=135 and substituting the instantaneous volume and volume rate; this is a direct differentiation application.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 6] The continuous random variable X has a probability distribution f defined as f(x) = (b/a)x, 0 ≤ x ≤ a; f(x) = b/(5 − a)(5 − x), a < x ≤ 5, where 0 < a < 5 and b ∈ ℚ. The graph of f is shown in the following diagram. The graph is a straight line from (0, 0) to (a, b), followed by a straight line down to (5, 0), with the point (a, b) indicated. (a) Show that b = 0.4. [2] It is given that E(X) = 3.2. (b) Find the value of a. [4]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: The density is f(x)=(b/a)x for 0≤x≤a and f(x)=b(5-x)/(5-a) for a<x≤5. The total area is 1, so (1/2)ab+(1/2)(5-a)b=(5/2)b=1, giving b=0.4. Using E(X)=3.2, ∫_0^a x(0.4x/a)dx + ∫_a^5 x[0.4(5-x)/(5-a)]dx = 3.2. Solving gives a=4.600000... . Hence a=4.6 and b=0.4.
records.consensusRationale: The density is normalized by area and its expected value is evaluated by piecewise integration; the variable is explicitly continuous.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 8] Consider the curve (x − d)² + (y − 2)² = 4 where x, y ∈ ℝ and d > 2, shown in the following diagram. The diagram shows a circle of radius 2 with centre (d, 2), tangent to the x-axis at (d, 0), with the y-axis to the left of the circle. The region enclosed by the curve is rotated through 2π radians around the y-axis to form a solid, S. (a) Show that the volume of S is given by 4πd ∫₀⁴ √(4 − (y − 2)²) dy. [6] It is given that the volume of S is 50π² cm³. (b) Find the value of d. [2]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText: From (x-d)²+(y-2)²=4, the right-hand semicircle is x=d+√(4-(y-2)²), while the left-hand semicircle is x=d-√(4-(y-2)²), for 0≤y≤4. Rotating the horizontal strip between them through 2π about the y-axis gives washers: V=π∫_0^4[(d+√(4-(y-2)²))²-(d-√(4-(y-2)²))²]dy = 4πd∫_0^4√(4-(y-2)²)dy. The integral is the area of a semicircle of radius 2, namely 2π, so V=8π²d. Given V=50π² cm³, d=50π²/(8π²)=25/4 cm.
records.consensusRationale: The required formula and final value are obtained by washer integration for a rotated circle region.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 30] This question considers different methods of summing powers of integers. The sum of the first n positive integers, each raised to the power zero, is given by S₀(n) = 1⁰ + 2⁰ + … + n⁰ where n ∈ ℤ⁺. (a) (i) Find the value of S₀(4). [1] (ii) Write down a simplified expression for S₀(n). [1] The sum of the first n positive integers, each raised to the power 1, is given by S₁(n) = 1¹ + 2¹ + … + n¹ where n ∈ ℤ⁺. (b) Use the fact that S₁(n) is the sum of n terms of an arithmetic sequence to show that S₁(n) = n²/2 + n/2. [3] The sum of the first n square numbers is given by S₂(n) = 1² + 2² + 3² … + n² where n ∈ ℤ⁺. (c) Find S₂(5). [1] (d) The following graph shows three rectangles, where the heights of the rectangles are consecutive square numbers, and the width of each rectangle is 1. The graph may be extended in a similar way to include any number of rectangles. The curve y = f(x) passes through the top right corner of each rectangle. Diagram description: coordinate axes x and y, with x marked 0, 1, 2 and 3 and y marked from 0 to 9; the curve y = f(x) passes through (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 4) and (3, 9); three shaded adjacent rectangles of width 1 occupy 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 with height 1, 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 with height 4, and 2 ≤ x ≤ 3 with height 9. (i) Write down an expression for f(x). [1] (ii) By considering the total area of the first n rectangles and the area under the curve, show that S₂(n) > n³/3. [4] (iii) Use a similar method to show that S₂(n) < n³/3 + n² + n. [4] The question continues on the following page. Consider the sequence uₙ = n³ − (n − 1)³ for n ∈ ℤ⁺. Some of the values of uₙ and Σᵣ₌₁ⁿ uᵣ are shown in the following table. Table columns: n, uₙ, Σᵣ₌₁ⁿ uᵣ. Rows: n = 1, uₙ = 1, sum = 1; n = 2, uₙ = 7, sum = 8; n = 3, uₙ = a, sum = b; n = 4, uₙ = 37, sum = 64. (e) Find the value of (i) a; [1] (ii) b. [1] (f) (i) Suggest an expression for Σᵣ₌₁ⁿ uᵣ in terms of n. [1] (ii) Use the definition of uₙ to prove that your suggestion is true. [3] (g) (i) Find a quadratic expression for uₙ. [2] (ii) Hence, write Σᵣ₌₁ⁿ uᵣ in terms of S₂(n), S₁(n) and S₀(n). [2] (iii) Hence, show that S₂(n) = n³/3 + n²/2 + n/6. [3] (iv) Show that the expression for S₂(n) given in (g)(iii) is consistent with the inequalities in part (d). [2]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText:
(a) (i) S₀(4) = 1⁰ + 2⁰ + 3⁰ + 4⁰ = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4.
(ii) There are n terms and every term is 1, so S₀(n) = n.
(b) The terms 1, 2, …, n form an arithmetic sequence with first term 1, last term n and n terms. Therefore S₁(n) = n/2(1 + n) = n²/2 + n/2.
(c) S₂(5) = 1² + 2² + 3² + 4² + 5² = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 = 55.
(d) (i) The curve passes through (k, k²) for each positive integer k, so f(x) = x².
(ii) The total area of the first n rectangles is S₂(n). Since x² is increasing on x ≥ 0, each right-endpoint rectangle lies above the curve. Hence S₂(n) > ∫₀ⁿ x² dx = [x³/3]₀ⁿ = n³/3.
(iii) Using the corresponding upper estimate (or integrating the quadratic comparison for the rectangles) gives S₂(n) < n³/3 + n² + n. Directly, the difference is n³/3 + n² + n − S₂(n) = n²/2 + 5n/6 > 0 for n ∈ Z⁺, so the stated inequality follows.
(e) (i) a = u₃ = 3³ − (3 − 1)³ = 27 − 8 = 19.
(ii) b = Σᵣ₌₁³ uᵣ = u₁ + u₂ + u₃ = 1 + 7 + 19 = 27 (equivalently, b = 64 − u₄ = 64 − 37).
(f) (i) Σᵣ₌₁ⁿ uᵣ = Σᵣ₌₁ⁿ [r³ − (r − 1)³] telescopes to n³ − 0³ = n³.
(ii) Proof by induction: for n = 1, Σᵣ₌₁¹uᵣ = u₁ = 1 = 1³. Assume Σᵣ₌₁ⁿuᵣ = n³. Then Σᵣ₌₁ⁿ⁺¹uᵣ = n³ + uₙ₊₁ = n³ + [(n + 1)³ − n³] = (n + 1)³. Thus the result holds for all n ∈ Z⁺.
(g) (i) uₙ = n³ − (n − 1)³ = n³ − (n³ − 3n² + 3n − 1) = 3n² − 3n + 1.
(ii) Σᵣ₌₁ⁿuᵣ = Σᵣ₌₁ⁿ(3r² − 3r + 1) = 3S₂(n) − 3S₁(n) + S₀(n).
(iii) From part (f)(i), n³ = 3S₂(n) − 3S₁(n) + S₀(n). Substituting S₁(n) = n²/2 + n/2 and S₀(n) = n gives 3S₂(n) = n³ + 3(n²/2 + n/2) − n = n³ + 3n²/2 + n/2. Therefore S₂(n) = n³/3 + n²/2 + n/6.
(iv) For the lower inequality, S₂(n) − n³/3 = n²/2 + n/6 > 0. For the upper inequality, (n³/3 + n² + n) − S₂(n) = n²/2 + 5n/6 > 0. Thus n³/3 < S₂(n) < n³/3 + n² + n, consistent with part (d).
records.consensusRationale: The dominant work derives and proves sums of powers, including a telescoping/induction proof; the rectangle bounds independently use area under a curve and integration.

records.questionText: [Maximum mark: 25] This question asks you to explore curves in the complex plane defined by r = a + b sin θ, where a and b are real constants. A complex number z can be represented by a point in the complex plane whose position is determined by the modulus, r, and the argument, θ, of z. The set of points which satisfy a given relationship between r and θ form a curve in the complex plane. Consider a family of curves defined by r = a + b sin θ, where a and b are real constants. First consider the case where a = 4 and b = 0 so that r = 4. The curve defined by r = 4 is the set of points in the complex plane which represent complex numbers with a modulus of 4. (a) Suppose that z is a complex number such that r = 4. Find all possible values of z such that (i) z is purely real; [1] (ii) z is purely imaginary; [1] (iii) the argument of z is π/4. [1] (b) Sketch the curve defined by r = 4 on an Argand diagram, showing clearly the values of the intercepts with the real and imaginary axes. [2] Now consider the case where a = 0 and b = 4 so that r = 4 sin θ, where 0 ≤ θ ≤ π. (c) Suppose that z is a complex number such that r = 4 sin θ, where 0 ≤ θ ≤ π. (i) Write down the greatest possible value of r. [1] (ii) For this value of r, find z. [2] (d) Use the identities x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ to show that the points on the curve defined by r = 4 sin θ lie on the curve x² + (y − 2)² = 4, where x = Re(z) and y = Im(z). [4] The question continues on the following page. (e) Consider the curve x² + (y − 2)² = 4. (i) Find an expression for dy/dx in terms of x and y. [3] (ii) Hence or otherwise, find the values of x for which the gradient of the curve is undefined. [2] (f) The curve defined by r = 4 sin θ, where 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, is a circle. Sketch this curve on an Argand diagram, showing clearly the values of any intercepts with the real and imaginary axes. [1] Finally, consider the case where a = 4 and b = 4. The curve defined by r = 4 + 4 sin θ, where 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, is shown on the following Argand diagram. The curve has a horizontal tangent at point A, point B and point C. The real parts of the numbers represented by A, B and C are negative, positive and zero, respectively. Diagram description: an Argand diagram with horizontal Re axis and vertical Im axis; the limacon r = 4 + 4 sin θ is drawn, passing through the origin, with a large upper loop reaching Im = 8 and extending from Re = −4 to Re = 4, and a small lower loop reaching approximately Im = −2; point A is on the lower loop at negative real part, point B is on the lower loop at positive real part, and point C is on the positive imaginary axis at Im = 8. (g) Use the identities x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ to show that the gradient of the curve at the point (r cos θ, r sin θ) is given by dy/dx = cos θ(1 + 2 sin θ)/(1 − sin θ − 2 sin² θ). [5] (h) Hence, find the value of θ which corresponds to the point A. [2]
records.markschemeOrSolutionText:
(a) (i) For r = 4, a purely real z has argument 0 or π, so z = 4e⁰ = 4 or z = 4eⁱπ = −4. Thus z = ±4.
(ii) A purely imaginary point on |z| = 4 has argument π/2 or 3π/2, so z = 4i or z = −4i. Thus z = ±4i.
(iii) If arg(z) = π/4, then z = 4(cos(π/4) + i sin(π/4)) = 4(√2/2 + i√2/2) = 2√2 + 2√2i.
(b) The locus r = 4 is the circle |z| = 4, centred at the origin with radius 4. Its intercepts are (4, 0), (−4, 0), (0, 4) and (0, −4); sketch this circle on an Argand diagram.
(c) (i) For r = 4 sin θ and 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, the greatest possible value of sin θ is 1, attained at θ = π/2. Hence r_max = 4.
(ii) At θ = π/2, z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = 4(0 + i) = 4i.
(d) With x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, r = 4 sin θ gives r² = 4r sin θ = 4y. Since r² = x² + y², x² + y² = 4y, so x² + (y − 2)² = 4. This is the circle centred at (0, 2) with radius 2.
(e) (i) Differentiate x² + (y − 2)² = 4 implicitly: 2x + 2(y − 2) dy/dx = 0. Therefore dy/dx = −x/(y − 2).
(ii) The gradient is undefined when y − 2 = 0, so y = 2. Substitution into x² + (y − 2)² = 4 gives x² = 4, hence x = ±2.
(f) The locus r = 4 sin θ is the circle x² + (y − 2)² = 4, centred at (0, 2) with radius 2. Its real-axis intercept is (0, 0); its imaginary-axis intercepts are (0, 0) and (0, 4). Sketch this circle on the Argand diagram.
(g) For r = 4 + 4 sin θ, x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ. Since dr/dθ = 4 cos θ, dx/dθ = (dr/dθ)cos θ − r sin θ = 4(1 − sin θ − 2 sin²θ), while dy/dθ = (dr/dθ)sin θ + r cos θ = 4 cos θ(1 + 2 sin θ). Therefore, wherever dx/dθ ≠ 0, dy/dx = (dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ) = cos θ(1 + 2 sin θ)/(1 − sin θ − 2 sin²θ).
(h) At A the tangent is horizontal, so dy/dx = 0. From the expression in (g), cos θ(1 + 2 sin θ) = 0. Point A is in the third quadrant and is not the top point, so cos θ ≠ 0 and 1 + 2 sin θ = 0. Thus sin θ = −1/2; in the third quadrant, θ = 7π/6.
records.consensusRationale: The locus is formulated in polar/complex-plane terms; implicit/parametric slope work is differentiation, while converting the loci to circle equations is coordinate analytic geometry.
